rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four usable editorial lanes and tells them exactly what would make each one stand up. Its best line is the pricing frame: “the story isn't the robot; it's the pairing,” which is the whole assignment in one clean sentence. B has useful bones, especially “Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why,” but it keeps leaning past the supplied facts with “call it a pilot, not a rollout” and “the industry's usual pattern of automation reducing headcount over time.”
gaps_in_A: “that's an architecture, and it's the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” overclaims from two facts; the update says Autocado is rolling out and Digital Makeline is being tested, not that Chipotle has proved a full-line architecture.
“Both the 100-restaurant rollout and the price-freeze commitment are live company news as of today; the two statements were made together” assumes announcement packaging not explicitly supplied.
The category angle could name its own ceiling sooner: 100 of 3,500+ and a separate system still only in testing make this a strategy question, not a proved category shift.
gaps_in_B: “call it a pilot, not a rollout” is a sharp headline, but it contradicts the supplied wording; the facts say Autocado is rolling out to 100 restaurants after pilot kitchens.
“the industry's usual pattern of automation reducing headcount over time” imports an outside claim without evidence from the update.
“Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout, making the two-system pattern visible for the first time” invents timing and novelty the update does not prove.
The next step is too timid: “No clean hand-off yet” underrates the set's own viable angles; a fit-checked trade or labor target could still be built around the stated proof gaps.
